content.text:
Yes. In the U.S., the clearest teaching shortages are not evenly spread across “academia”; they cluster in particular **school subjects, professional fields, and locations**.

**Common shortage areas:**

- **Special education** — one of the most persistent shortages; reported by 45 states in 2024–25 data. ([learningpolicyinstitute.org](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-shortages-subjects-across-states-factsheet?utm_source=openai))  
- **Science** — especially middle/high school physical science, chemistry, physics, and general STEM; reported by 41 states. ([learningpolicyinstitute.org](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-shortages-subjects-across-states-factsheet?utm_source=openai))  
- **Mathematics** — reported by 40 states. ([learningpolicyinstitute.org](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-shortages-subjects-across-states-factsheet?utm_source=openai))  
- **World languages / bilingual education / TESOL** — many districts struggle to find certified teachers, especially for less commonly taught languages and English learner support. The U.S. Department of Education specifically lists math, science, foreign languages, and bilingual education among shortage areas relevant to loan-cancellation rules. ([ed.gov](https://www.ed.gov/teaching-and-administration/professional-development/teacher-shortage-areas?utm_source=openai))  
- **Career and technical education** — e.g., skilled trades, computer science, engineering technology, health occupations, agriculture, and industry-linked programs. SREB notes that career and technical education remains a steady shortage category across states. ([sreb.org](https://www.sreb.org/post/teacher-shortage-area-data?utm_source=openai))  
- **Nursing education / nurse faculty** — at the college level, nursing schools often cannot admit all qualified applicants because there are not enough faculty, clinical sites, preceptors, and related resources. AACN reported that U.S. nursing schools turned away over 80,000 qualified applications in 2024 for those reasons. ([aacnnursing.org](https://www.aacnnursing.org/news-data/fact-sheets/nursing-faculty-shortage?utm_source=openai))  

Fields that are **less likely** to have shortages, depending heavily on region, often include areas such as history, social studies, English literature, some humanities, and some arts fields—especially at the college level, where there can be many PhDs competing for relatively few tenure-track jobs.

A useful way to think about it: there are shortages where teaching requires a skillset that is also valuable outside education. **Math, science, computer science, engineering, nursing, trades, and special education** all have strong non-teaching labor markets or demanding credential requirements, so schools often struggle to compete.
